summary.title: Practical Dependent Types in Haskell: Type-Safe Neural Networks (Part 1)
summary.one_liner: You learn how to move a feed-forward neural network with back-propagation from runtime-checked matrices to size-indexed types in Haskell, so the compiler catches dimension mismatches.
takeaways: Start with simple types, find partial functions and bugs, then refine types to make the compiler enforce matrix dimensions.
Encode weight matrix sizes in types (Weights i o, R n, L m n) so incompatible layers fail to compile.
Use GADTs and type-level lists of Nats to describe a whole network's input, hidden, and output shapes.
Singletons and induction are needed to build networks from type-level information at runtime, since types are erased in Haskell.
summary.summary: The post is part 1 of a series on practical dependent types in Haskell, aimed at intermediate programmers. It starts with an untyped feed-forward neural network using hmatrix and walks through its back-propagation training, then examines where partial functions and unchecked dimensions cause bugs. It then reworks the design with size-indexed types (Weights i o, Network i hs o, KnownNat constraints) using hmatrix's Static module, showing how type inference generates correctly sized weights. The post ends by introducing singletons and induction to construct networks from type-level lists.
